title: Parents’ Attachment in Conversation with their  Children: Impacts on their emotions and the relationship
abstract: Insecure attachment has well­documented implications for emotional functioning in romantic relationships, yet little research has explored how attachment (of the parent) may impact parent­ child relationships. The present laboratory­based study examined whether parents’ (N = 26; Mage = 48) attachment insecurity was related to emotions they and their children (Mage = 17) experienced during conversations. Parents’ insecure attachment (a composite of avoidant and anxious attachment; alpha = .85) was measured using the Adult Attachment Questionnaire. Parents and children engaged in (1) a neutral conversation about events of the day, (2) a conflict conversation about a topic of disagreement, and (3) a positive conversation about a topic of mutual enjoyment and reported on their emotional experiences after each conversation. In terms of parent’s attachment predicting their own experience, results showed that higher levels of parents’ insecure attachment were associated with higher levels of negative emotional experiences during the conflict conversation (r = 0.48, p= 0.015). This finding generalized across both anxious and avoidant attachment; was driven by negative emotions (e.g., anger); and was specific to the conflict conversation. In terms of parent’s attachment predicting their child’s experience, higher levels of avoidant attachment (and not overall insecure or anxious attachment) were associated with lower levels of positive emotions reported by their child (i.e., amusement, r = ­0.46, p = 0.022; excitement, r= ­0.43, p = 0.031). These findings highlight the downstream effects that parents’ attachment insecurity has on their own emotional functioning when navigating disagreements with their children and their children’s positive experiences.
